analysis.one_liner: Requires every state to guarantee health insurance to all residents, funded by tobacco, cosmetics, and high-income taxes.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have required every state to guarantee health coverage to all residents by 1995, was referred to House committees in early 1990 and died without a hearing or a vote when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every state to put a universal health insurance plan in place by January 1, 1995. Employers with 25 or more workers would have had to cover their employees and families, states would have had to sell affordable coverage to poor and uninsurable people at premiums based on income, and Medicaid would have had to meet national minimum standards. The plan would have been paid for by doubling federal tobacco taxes, creating a new 50% tax on cosmetics, and raising the top income tax rate to 29%.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly tens of millions of uninsured Americans at the time: they would have gained guaranteed coverage, a ban on preexisting-condition exclusions, caps on premiums and out-of-pocket costs, and income-based premiums for those unable to buy insurance. Small-business employees, the self-employed, and the unemployed would have gained insurance pools designed to lower their costs. Medicaid recipients would have gained national minimum eligibility and coverage standards. Providers would have gained from fewer unpaid bills.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The uninsured and people with preexisting conditions

how_it_helps.text: Required every state to have a health insurance plan covering all residents operating by January 1, 1995, with employers of 25 or more people enrolling employees and their families and the state covering low-income, preexisting-condition, and otherwise uninsurable people at premiums proportional to income.

Prohibited health plans in the state system from excluding or limiting anyone because of a preexisting condition, and capped premiums, deductibles, copayments, and coinsurance individuals could be charged.

Required every covered plan to include hospital care, physician services, diagnostic tests, prenatal and well-baby care, mental health care, and long-term nursing home and home health care, with no dollar or duration limits on core benefits.
Created insurance pools and other mechanisms to make coverage affordable for the self-employed, the unemployed, and employees of businesses with fewer than 25 workers.

Directed the Health and Human Services Secretary to set national minimum Medicaid eligibility and coverage standards, and made continued federal Medicaid payments conditional on each state adopting an approved universal coverage plan.

Paid for it all through a dedicated Universal Health Coverage Trust Fund fed by higher tobacco and cosmetics excise taxes and a new 29% rate on incomes above the phaseout of the 15% rate and personal exemptions, which CRS describes as eliminating a marginal tax reduction for the wealthy.
Amended ERISA so that state laws carrying out the plan could reach self-insured employer plans, closing the usual escape hatch large employers use to avoid state coverage rules.

analysis.who_pays: Tobacco users, whose federal excise taxes would have doubled (for example, cigarettes from $8 to $16 per thousand and cigars from 75 cents to $1.50), and tobacco companies; cosmetics buyers and manufacturers, through a new 50% excise tax on cosmetics; high-income households, through a 29% top marginal rate; and employers with 25 or more workers, who would have had to pay to enroll employees and their families in qualifying health plans.
analysis.who_pays_short: Tobacco users, cosmetics buyers, high earners, employers

drawbacks.text: The tobacco tax doubling would have fallen on smokers, who skew toward lower incomes, making a significant share of the financing regressive; the new 50% cosmetics tax would also land on everyday shoppers rather than only the wealthy.
Employers with 25 or more workers would have faced a new mandate to pay for family coverage for employees and dependents, a real cost that could show up in wages or hiring at the margin.

States had to comply by January 1, 1995 or lose federal Medicaid payments, with only narrow hardship waivers, which put a heavy and partly unfunded burden on state governments to design and run their own plans.

The bill kept private insurance as the delivery channel rather than creating a single public plan, so administrative costs and insurer overhead would have remained in the system; it also excluded routine physicals and most preventive care from the required benefit package.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside was large: guaranteed coverage for everyone in a state, a preexisting-condition ban, and income-based premiums, financed mostly by tobacco, cosmetics, and high-income taxes rather than by middle-class taxpayers. The honest costs are the regressive tobacco taxes, a new mandate on mid-size and large employers, and a stiff deadline backed by the threat of cutting off Medicaid money to noncomplying states. The design left the private insurance industry in place as the delivery system, which moderated savings but also made it less disruptive. On balance, this was a broad attempt to extend coverage that traded new taxes and employer costs for universal protection.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to two House committees, which split it among three subcommittees, and it sat there until the Congress ended without a hearing, a markup, or any vote.

narrative.text: Representative David Obey, joined only by Representative Jim McDermott, introduced the Universal Health Coverage Act of 1990 on January 30, 1990.
The same day, the House referred it jointly to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee.

In early February 1990 it was further referred to the Subcommittee on Health, the Subcommittee on Health and the Environment, and the Subcommittee on Commerce, Consumer Protection and Competitiveness.
No hearing, markup, floor action, or vote ever appears in the record, and the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991 with the bill dead.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco companies, cosmetics manufacturers, high-income households, and large employers were spared the new taxes and coverage mandates the bill would have imposed. The uninsured gained nothing; the country would wait until the Affordable Care Act two decades later for a comparable preexisting-condition ban and coverage expansion.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Tobacco and cosmetics industries; the uninsured stayed uninsured

for.name: Rep. Jim McDermott
for.what_they_did: Joined Obey as the bill's only cosponsor at introduction.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so there is no roll-call record; the only support in the record is two House Democrats, with no Republican cosponsor.

industries.note: By mandating that employers of 25 or more workers buy qualifying private plans and that states build coverage pools, the bill would have funneled millions of new customers into private insurance while subjecting those plans to required benefits, premium caps, a ban on preexisting-condition exclusions, and ERISA changes closing the self-insurance loophole. Insurers' role as the gatekeeper of coverage would have been locked in even as they faced new rules.
Federal excise taxes would have doubled across cigars, cigarettes, and smokeless tobacco, with a floor-stocks tax on inventory, directly raising costs for the industry and prices for smokers.
A brand-new 50% manufacturer-level excise tax on cosmetics would have been one of the steepest federal excise rates ever applied to a consumer product category.

Employers with 25 or more employees would have been required to enroll workers and their families in compliant health plans, a substantial new benefit cost, and the ERISA amendment would have removed their ability to self-insure around state rules.
A new 29% rate would have applied to income above the phaseout of the 15% bracket and personal exemptions, directly targeting wealthy taxpayers to finance coverage.

Universal coverage means far fewer uninsured patients and less uncompensated care, so providers would have gained paying patients alongside the new mental health and long-term care coverage requirements.
